item.title: New ageing policy takes shape, says Saurogo
item.description: AFTER a gap of 10 years, Fiji is reviewing its National Ageing Policy through extensive nationwide consultations, says Women in Art and Climate Action (WACA) administrator Paulini Saurogo. Speaking at a Women in Art and Climate Action (WACA) Roundtable discussion in Lautoka last week, Ms Saurogo said the draft National Ageing Policy 2026-2035 is taking shape, as it involves more than 1700 particip
item.content:encoded:
AFTER a gap of 10 years, Fiji is reviewing its National Ageing Policy through extensive nationwide consultations, says Women in Art and Climate Action (WACA) administrator Paulini Saurogo.

Speaking at a Women in Art and Climate Action (WACA) Roundtable discussion in Lautoka last week, Ms Saurogo said the draft National Ageing Policy 2026-2035 is taking shape, as it involves more than 1700 participants involved in more than 100 sessions.

“The draft policy is structured around six priority areas – social protection, health and caregiving, transport and accessibility, digital inclusion, community infrastructure and disaster preparedness, and legal protection,” she said.

“The government is also exploring a dedicated legislative framework to better protect elderly citizens, studying international models where assets transferred by older persons can legally revert if they are subsequently neglected.

“Existing laws, including the Family Law Act, the Domestic Violence Act, and the Crimes Act, already provide legal safeguards – but enforcement and early reporting remain critical.”

Ms Saurogo said the roundtable discussion that brought together community leaders, elder care representatives, faith leaders, and local stakeholders serves two core purposes.

“First, we are here to provide a platform for local voices – elder care providers, faith leaders, educators, and civil society — to deliberate on the current challenges facing Fiji’s ageing population and to outline a vision for a future where seniors live with dignity, security and respect.

“Second, we stand in solidarity with international humanitarian efforts calling for the release of chairman Man Hee Lee, a 95-year-old peace activist and war veteran currently detained under deeply concerning humanitarian conditions in South Korea.”

The roundtable discussion was hosted by the Women in Art and Climate Action (WACA). It highlighted challenges facing Fiji’s ageing population and promoting compassionate, lawful, and inclusive approaches to elder care, justice, and universal human rights.

item.title: Chiefly authority must be respected – Tui Mali
item.description: RESPECT for traditional leadership and village protocols must be upheld to preserve the rights and authority of the iTaukei chiefly system, says Tui Mali Ratu Apenisa Bogiso. Ratu Apenisa said some laws introduced in previous years had weakened the authority of traditional leaders and affected the way villages governed themselves.
item.content:encoded:
RESPECT for traditional leadership and village protocols must be upheld to preserve the rights and authority of the iTaukei chiefly system, says Tui Mali Ratu Apenisa Bogiso.

Ratu Apenisa said some laws introduced in previous years had weakened the authority of traditional leaders and affected the way villages governed themselves.

“Some of those laws weakened the authority of the traditional system,” he said.

He supported a call by the Roko Tui Dreketi, Ro Teimumu Kepa, to review more than 30 laws from the previous government. They argue these laws harm indigenous iTaukei rights and organisations.

For example, the 2007 decree unfairly ended the Great Council of Chiefs, while the 2013 Constitution hurt traditional land and fishing rights.

He said the iTaukei system already had established processes for making decisions and resolving issues within communities.

“In our villages, we already have our own proper way of making decisions.”

He said anyone entering a village should observe customary protocols by respecting the chief and following traditional practices.

“When people come into the village, they should listen, respect the chief and follow the proper protocol.”

He said the authority of the chief remained central to maintaining order, unity and respect within village communities.

“When the chief speaks, people should listen. That is our way.”

He said protecting the role of traditional leaders was important for preserving iTaukei customs, identity and cultural values for future generations while maintaining harmony within village life.

item.title: Pensioners seek justice | Remove constitutional barriers blocking legal challenges – Prof Naidu
item.description: THE 2012 Pensioners Committee has called on the Constitution Review Commission (CRC) to remove provisions that prevent citizens from challenging certain decrees and laws made during the 2006 to 2014 period. Committee chairman Professor Vijay Naidu said the provisions under Sections 173(3), 173(4) and 173(5) of the 2013 Constitution should be removed as they prevented courts from reviewing the lega
item.content:encoded:
THE 2012 Pensioners Committee has called on the Constitution Review Commission (CRC) to remove provisions that prevent citizens from challenging certain decrees and laws made during the 2006 to 2014 period.

Committee chairman Professor Vijay Naidu said the provisions under Sections 173(3), 173(4) and 173(5) of the 2013 Constitution should be removed as they prevented courts from reviewing the legality or constitutionality of certain laws and from granting remedies to affected people.

The submission stems from the 2011 Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) pension reforms, which reduced pension payments for existing pensioners.

A group of affected pensioners, led by the late David Burness, took legal action in the High Court challenging the reforms. The case had commenced, with Justice Hettiarachchi ruling that the proceedings would continue.

However, the then government later introduced the 2011 FNPF Transition Decree (Decree 51), which prevented courts from hearing challenges against the pension reforms or providing compensation, damages, relief or other remedies to affected pensioners.

In its submission to the CRC, the committee described Decree 51 as a violation of the rights of pensioners affected by the reforms.

“The 2012 Pensioners Committee maintains that Decree 51 was a gross violation of the human rights of approximately 6000 pensioners at that time,” Prof Naidu said.

“This number has dwindled down to approximately 1400 as more than 4600 have died without seeing pension justice done.”

Prof Naidu acknowledged that the Coalition Government, through former Minister of Finance Prof Biman Prasad, had provided pension top-ups using taxpayer funds over the past year and a half for some affected pensioners.

“The remaining pensioners continue to wait for full pension justice amid their struggles to make ends meet.”

The committee’s submission called for the removal of provisions that restrict courts from hearing cases related to laws made between December 5, 2006 and the first sitting of Parliament under the 2013 Constitution.

Prof Naidu said the restrictions preventing citizens from seeking legal remedies should be removed, while provisions that did not limit access to justice should remain.

“The 2012 Pensioners Committee’s specific request is that those following sections be removed from the anticipated Constitution of the Republic of Fiji.”

item.title: Inter-cropping viable with right resources says Dass
item.description: INTER-CROPPING is an option for sugarcane farmers, but they must be provided the right resources to allow for diversification said Nawaicoba sector farmer Bala Dass. Mr Dass, who is chairperson of the Lautoka Cane Producers Association, said he had planted and harvested watermelon last year but would not be planting anymore soon.
item.content:encoded:
INTER-CROPPING is an option for sugarcane farmers, but they must be provided the right resources to allow for diversification said Nawaicoba sector farmer Bala Dass.

Mr Dass, who is chairperson of the Lautoka Cane Producers Association, said he had planted and harvested watermelon last year but would not be planting anymore soon.

“We need proper irrigation for growing other crops,” he said.

“I planted watermelon and they turned out very well but after a few months, the weather got too dry.

“Proper irrigation was the main problem.”

According to the association many growers planted vegetables between sugar cane plots.

Mr Dass said the changing weather patterns had affected farmers’ ability to diversify.

“We are having drier weather and more rain and floods. So, it affects our vegetables farms.

“The difference is sugar cane mostly can survive these types of change in weather.”

Greenfield Mechanical Harvester Cooperative Ltd chairperson Krishna Murti Gounder said inter-cropping was for manual labour dependent growers.

“For mechanical harvesters it will be difficult for us because we’ve spent thousands of dollars on these machines,” Mr Gounder said.

“We have to grow sugar cane to be able to make our money back.”

item.title: Rate drop affects operations
item.description: A SUGARCANE mechanical harvester operator in Labasa will stop service after the operating price dropped yesterday. The previous mechanical harvesting rate of $18.90 per tonne was reviewed and increased to $24.63 per tonne, a 30.3 per cent increase, effective from June 23, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
A SUGARCANE mechanical harvester operator in Labasa will stop service after the operating price dropped yesterday.

The previous mechanical harvesting rate of $18.90 per tonne was reviewed and increased to $24.63 per tonne, a 30.3 per cent increase, effective from June 23, 2026.

However, it dropped to $20.52 per tonne last month.

The review was made following increased fuel prices and rising operating costs faced by harvesting operators.

Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna said the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) should be approached for further information regarding the review of mechanical harvesting rates.

“The funds allocated to the ministry were intended to support transportation costs until the end of August and were not for reviewing mechanical harvesting rates,” he said.

Mr Tunabuna said the review and approval of harvesting charges remained the responsibility of the FCCC.

However, Bucaisau mechanical harvester operator Firoz Ali said operators could not continue working if they were forced back to the previous rate.

“We cannot afford to continue paying at this rate during harvesting. We are being paid $24.63, but in the end, we are only receiving $18.90, and nothing has been given from the FSC policy,” he said.

Mr Ali said this had created uncertainty among operators.

FCCC’s chief executive officer Senikavika Jiuta said the decrease was primarily driven by a decline in fuel prices, which are a significant component in both harvesting and cartage operations.

Ms Jiuta said the adjustment reflected the organisation’s commitment to maintaining fairness.

item.title: Equipment to boost organic farming
item.description: ORGANIC farming communities across Fiji are better equipped to grow healthy food and strengthen resilient agro-ecological farming systems. This follows the distribution of essential farm support tools to 195 organic farmers under the Pacific Organic Learning Farms Network project.
item.content:encoded:
ORGANIC farming communities across Fiji are better equipped to grow healthy food and strengthen resilient agro-ecological farming systems.

This follows the distribution of essential farm support tools to 195 organic farmers under the Pacific Organic Learning Farms Network project.

Implemented by the Pacific Community, the project provided spades, wheelbarrows, watering cans, pruning shears, compost bins, fencing materials, shade cloths, knapsack sprayers and other tools to support daily farming activities and sustainable production.

Project manager Fuatino Fatiaki said the support was designed to make farming more efficient for households that may struggle to afford basic equipment.

“This also helps in improving access to equipment for farming households that may struggle to afford essential tools,” Ms Fatiaki said.

“The project is also helping farmers focus on building productive and sustainable farms.”

She said strengthening farm clusters was important for building communities that could withstand future challenges.

“Agro-ecological farming systems are designed to support farmers sustainably over the long term.”

“Recent global events, including the COVID-19 pandemic and rising fuel costs, have shown how vulnerable our food systems can be.”

Burenitu Village farmer Meli Nacola said the distribution had inspired farmers to continue their organic farming journey.

“Receiving these farm support tools has really boosted the morale of our farmers,” Mr Nacola said.

“It has encouraged many of us to continue our transition to organic farming.”

item.title: Call to diversify farming
item.description: The Ra Provincial Council has backed calls for farmers to diversify into alternative crops as rural communities adjust to the closure of the Penang Sugar Mill and rising cane transportation costs. Council chairman Kiniviliame Salabogi said farmers needed to explore commercial opportunities beyond traditional sugar cane farming, supporting Assistant Minister for Justice Josaia Niudamu’s call during
item.content:encoded:
The Ra Provincial Council has backed calls for farmers to diversify into alternative crops as rural communities adjust to the closure of the Penang Sugar Mill and rising cane transportation costs.

Council chairman Kiniviliame Salabogi said farmers needed to explore commercial opportunities beyond traditional sugar cane farming, supporting Assistant Minister for Justice Josaia Niudamu’s call during the national budget debate for greater investment in crops such as dalo, kava, cassava and coffee.

Mr Salabogi said farmers were now looking at expanding these activities on a larger scale rather than limiting production to small household farms.

“In regards to dalo and kava, we are looking at venturing more into these forms of farming on a larger scale,” he said.

He said rising costs associated with transporting cane, particularly from areas such as Nalawa to Ba, had reduced returns for farmers and encouraged them to seek alternative sources of income.

The shift towards diversification is already gaining traction, with coffee farming expanding in Ra through initiatives such as Onna Coffee’s investment in Rakiraki and surrounding villages.

Mr Niudamu said Ra’s agricultural future depended on a managed transition towards high-value crops, including coffee, cowpea and beans, which could strengthen food security, create jobs and provide new income opportunities.

He said Government and partner organisations would continue supporting farmers as they adapt to changing conditions in the agriculture sector.

item.title: MP calls for emergency funding for boat safety beacons
item.description: Opposition Member of Parliament Rinesh Sharma is calling on the Government to immediately allocate at least $100,000 to equip Government boats with personal locator beacons, saying the recent rescue of six health workers in Lau exposed serious gaps in maritime safety. Mr Sharma said the funding should be used to install personal locator beacons on at least 200 Government vessels used by public ser
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Member of Parliament Rinesh Sharma is calling on the Government to immediately allocate at least $100,000 to equip Government boats with personal locator beacons, saying the recent rescue of six health workers in Lau exposed serious gaps in maritime safety.

Mr Sharma said the funding should be used to install personal locator beacons on at least 200 Government vessels used by public servants travelling across Fiji’s maritime waters.

His call follows the ordeal of six members of the Ministry of Health’s Ono-i-Lau outreach team, whose boat suffered engine failure and began taking on water while travelling from Moce to Oneata. The team survived by wearing life jackets and using the vessel’s wooden floor planks as flotation devices before being rescued about a day and a half later by the crew of Goundar Shipping Services’ Lomaiviti Princess 12 .

“Let us be very clear about what saved these six Fijians. It was not technology. It was not a system. It was a passing ferry and the good eyes of its crew,” Mr Sharma said.

“Our medical officer, our dental officer, our charge nurse, our peer educator, our health inspector and our dental assistant floated in the open Pacific for a day and a half because there was no way for anyone to know where they were.”

Mr Sharma said a registered personal locator beacon costs less than $900 and would significantly improve the chances of a rapid rescue.

“Activated in the water, it transmits an exact position to search and rescue satellites within minutes. Those six would have been located before dark on the first day. This is just one of the devices and I am sure there are more which the Ministry can procure.”

He noted that the 2026-2027 National Budget allocated $647 million to the health sector, including $477 million to the Ministry of Health for salaries, medicines, medical supplies and biomedical equipment.

“One hundred thousand dollars is one hundredth of one percent of that allocation. It is not a question of affordability. It is a question of whether we have thought about it at all.”

Mr Sharma said the proposed funding should cover the installation of beacons on Government vessels, registration of the devices to both boats and travelling officers, training in their use, and a replacement programme for ageing fibreglass punts used for outreach work.

“We ask nurses and doctors to cross the Lau waters to serve Fijians who would otherwise see no health worker at all. We send them out in small fibreglass punts. The least we owe them is a boat that can take the sea and a beacon that brings them home.”

“Fiji got lucky. Luck is not a maritime safety policy.”
